2027-07-07.title: Wednesday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: A divine jealousy: betrothed to one husband, to be presented to Christ; beware of another Jesus
“Let us go to Judea again”: Lazarus has fallen asleep, and Thomas says, “Let us also go, that we may die with him”
2027-07-07.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. The Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha was kept on Saturday, 3 July, and the Gospel today shows Thomas as a loyal and courageous friend.
2027-07-07.verse: Let us also go, that we may die with him.
theo: St Paul writes to the Corinthians with a feeling that he himself calls “a divine jealousy”: “I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The picture is a betrothal. In the Bible the love of God for his people is often told as a marriage (Hosea 2:19–20), and Paul sees himself as the friend of the bridegroom whose task is to bring the bride to him and to guard her faithfulness (John 3:29). His fear is not that the Corinthians will openly deny Christ but that they will be led astray little by little: “I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.” The serpent did not at first ask Eve to reject God; he asked a clever question. In the same way, Paul says, a stranger may come and proclaim “another Jesus than the one we proclaimed,” “a different spirit,” “a different gospel”, and the people “submit to it readily enough.” In our days voices about Jesus reach us from every side, from pulpits, screens and forwarded messages, and the question is the same: is this the Jesus whom the Apostles proclaimed, the Jesus of the Gospels and the Creed, who is the Son of God, died and rose? We ask it humbly, without contempt for anyone who sincerely seeks him; we ask it chiefly of ourselves, so that our own devotion remains simple and pure.

The Gospel begins when Jesus, having waited two days after hearing that Lazarus was ill, says to his disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.” The disciples are afraid: “Rabbi, the Jews were just now trying to stone you, and are you going there again?” (When John writes “the Jews” here he means some of the people and leaders of Judea who were hostile on that occasion; Jesus and his disciples were Jews themselves, and the Church does not blame the Jewish people as a whole for what happened to him: Nostra Aetate 4.) Jesus answers with a riddle about the day: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? Those who walk during the day do not stumble, because they see the light of this world. But those who walk at night stumble, because the light is not in them.” The hours of Jesus are measured by the Father's will. Whoever walks with him walks in daylight, even on a dangerous road, and cannot stumble; whoever walks without him walks in the dark, even on a smooth one. Then he says: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to awaken him.” The disciples take this for ordinary sleep and are relieved. “Then Jesus told them plainly, ‘Lazarus is dead.’”

Christians speak of the dead as those who have fallen asleep. The Greek word for a burial ground, koimeterion, from which we get “cemetery”, means a sleeping-place. St Augustine puts it in a phrase: to the Lord Lazarus was asleep, though to men he was dead, for the Lord could wake him as easily as one wakes a sleeper (Tractate on John 49, in substance). We do not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And then the most unexpected voice speaks: “Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, ‘Let us also go, that we may die with him.’” Only four days ago, on Saturday, we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, the Apostle whom our tradition says carried the Gospel to India. Most people remember him for one doubt after the Resurrection, but here he speaks first and bravely. He does not understand what the Lord is about to do; he is gloomy, and he is ready to die. He goes. St Paul wished the Corinthians a sincere and pure devotion; Thomas shows what it looks like, a love that follows the Lord to Judea, to the tomb and to the end, even before it understands. The Lord says, “For your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Let us also go.
outline: Ask: where am I afraid to follow the Lord today, and what would it mean to say “Let us also go”?
Point 1 · One husband, a pure devotion
Paul's divine jealousy; the danger of another Jesus; keeping our devotion simple.
Twelve hours of daylight: whoever walks with Jesus does not stumble; Lazarus is asleep.
Thomas the Twin, brave before he understands; the Dukrono we kept on Saturday.
“Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
live: Test what you hear or read about Jesus this week against the Gospel and the Creed, and put aside what does not match.
Begin one task you have been putting off because of fear, saying a short prayer first: “Lord, I walk with you.”
Go this week to visit a grieving person or a sick one, even if you do not know what to say; your presence is a way of saying “Let us go.”
2027-07-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, bridegroom of your Church, you wish to present her to the Father without spot or wrinkle. Keep us in a sincere and pure devotion to you, and guard us from every other Jesus, every different spirit and every different gospel. Let us walk with you in the light of day, never stumbling, and never afraid to follow you even to Judea. Give us the courage of your Apostle Thomas, who said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him,” and who carried your name to distant lands. Be with those who grieve, as you were with Martha and Mary, and awaken all who have fallen asleep in you. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church, the bride, is united with her Bridegroom in the one Body, and she is given strength to walk with him to Judea, to the Cross and to the tomb, believing that those who sleep in him will be awakened.

quick: St Paul feels a divine jealousy for the Corinthians: he has betrothed them to one husband, Christ, and fears that another Jesus may lead them astray.
Jesus says that whoever walks in daylight does not stumble; Lazarus has fallen asleep and Jesus goes to awaken him.
Thomas the Twin says: “Let us also go, that we may die with him”, a brave friend, whom we remembered on Saturday.
2027-07-07.action: Choose one fear that keeps you from following the Lord this week and say, “Let us also go.”
2027-07-07.question: Where is the Lord going that I am afraid to follow?

family.explain: When Jesus said that he wanted to go back to Judea, the disciples were afraid, because some people there wanted to hurt him. Jesus told them that whoever walks in the daylight does not trip. Then one friend spoke up: Thomas, who was called the Twin. He said that they should go too and be with Jesus, even if it was hard. He was brave. Last Saturday we remembered St Thomas, who, our tradition says, came all the way to India. The Lord was going to a sad house to awaken his friend Lazarus, who had fallen asleep in death.
family.intention: We pray for families who are sad because someone has died, and that we may be brave friends of Jesus like Thomas.
family.ask: Ask: “When is it hard to follow Jesus? Let us say together: Lord, we will go with you.”

illus: One monsoon night a landslide closed the road above Munnar, and a message came to a young catechism teacher that an old man in a lonely hamlet was dying and wanted the priest. The road was dangerous and the rain was heavy. The teacher's friends hesitated. She said, “Let us go, we can walk the last part,” and two of them agreed. They walked for two hours with a torch and one umbrella, found the old man still alive and prayed beside him until the priest arrived at dawn by another route. Afterwards she said she had not felt brave at all; she had only felt that she could not let him die with no one beside him. When the others asked what had made her say it, she remembered the line from the Gospel about Thomas, which she had read that week.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, light of the world, you walk before us in the day. Give us a pure and simple devotion to you, and the courage to say with Thomas, “Let us also go.” Amen.
share: I am afraid that your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3). What could lead my devotion away from simplicity?
Those who walk during the day do not stumble (John 11:9). When has walking with the Lord kept me from falling?
Let us also go (John 11:16). Whose side am I asked to stand beside, even when I am afraid?
pm.resp: Lord, we will go with you.
interc: For the Church, the bride of Christ, that she may remain faithful and pure in her devotion to him.
For all who are tempted by another gospel, that they may return to the Jesus of the Apostles.
For the sick and the dying, and for those who grieve, that they may feel the nearness of the Lord.
For the Church in India, that she may have the courage of Mar Thoma Shleeha.
For each of us, that we may follow the Lord to wherever he is going.
pm.close: Father, in your Son you have shown us the way, the light of the day, and in your Apostle Thomas the courage to follow him. Keep us faithful and bring us, with all who sleep in him, to the day that has no evening. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, in today's Epistle St Paul speaks of a divine jealousy. He has betrothed the Corinthians to one husband, to present them as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). He is afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, their thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3). Another Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel: people accept such things readily enough (2 Corinthians 11:4). In our own days many voices speak about Jesus; we must test them against the Gospel and the Creed, and keep our own devotion simple.

In the Gospel Jesus says, Let us go to Judea again (John 11:7). The disciples are afraid, since people there had lately tried to stone Jesus. Jesus says that there are twelve hours of daylight, and those who walk by day do not stumble because they see the light of this world (John 11:9). Whoever walks with Jesus walks by day. He adds: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to awaken him (John 11:11). For Christians death is a sleep from which the Lord awakens us.

And then Thomas speaks: Let us also go, that we may die with him (John 11:16). It is the bravest sentence the disciples say in this chapter. On Saturday we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, and today we see him follow his Lord, without understanding everything, to Judea and to the tomb.
Let us ask the Lord for a pure devotion and for the courage of Thomas, so that whenever he goes before us we may say, Let us also go. Amen.
kids: Children, do you remember the Apostle Thomas, whose feast we kept last Saturday? Today we hear about a brave thing he did. Jesus said that he was going to a place where some people wanted to hurt him. The other friends were afraid, but Thomas said: “Let us also go!” He did not want to leave Jesus alone. We can be like Thomas. When a friend is sad, when someone is sick, or when it is hard to do the right thing, we can say, “Let us also go; Jesus is with us.” Let us ask Jesus to make us brave friends.

intro: Theme: “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”
On Wednesday of the seventh week after Pentecost: a pure devotion to the one Bridegroom, walking in the daylight of the Lord, and the courage of Thomas the Twin.

sub: Keeping our devotion simple and sincere.
q: And I will take you for my wife forever; I will take you for my wife in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love, and in mercy.
He who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice.
points.apply: Test one thing you have heard about Jesus this week against the Gospel and the Creed.

sub: Whoever walks with Jesus does not stumble.
Lazarus has fallen asleep: death is a sleep that the Lord awakens.
q: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness but will have the light of life.
points.apply: Begin one task you have been postponing out of fear, saying: “Lord, I walk with you.”

sub: Thomas the Twin, brave before he understands.
The Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, kept on Saturday.
Going to the grieving and the dying.
q: Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.
points.apply: Visit a sick or grieving person this week and let your presence say: “Let us go.”

concl: The Church is betrothed to one Bridegroom; let us guard a simple and pure devotion to the Jesus of the Apostles.
Whoever walks with Jesus walks in the daylight and can say with Thomas: Let us also go.
2027-07-07.resolve: Keep your devotion pure, walk in the daylight with the Lord, and say with Thomas: Let us also go.
